Using Cannabis for Pain Relief in Debilitating Illness
By Dr. William Notcutt, FRCA, Consultant Anaesthetist, James Paget Hospital , Gorleston
GREAT YARMOUTH , Norfolk NR31 7EB UK

Cannabis and Patient Trials

Speculation is mounting that cannabis could be decriminalised for medical use within the next few years, opening up a whole new field of therapeutics.
(MarijuanaNews note: As this article makes clear below, there is no need for decriminalization for the medical use of cannabis, or its extracts.)

Full-scale patient trials are already under way with 2,000 patients participating. Dr. Dennis Chaplin visited James Paget Hospital in Norfolk, in order to gain some early insights from pioneer triallist Dr.William Notcutt. (MarijuanaNews note: It is my understanding that the 2,000 patients have not yet been recruited.)

Pain relief consultant Dr William Notcutt concedes that a degree of controversy is bound to follow his work to use cannabis in medical research under the auspices of the Medicines Control Agency.

His Great Yarmouth pain relief clinic, one of the British centres licensed to conduct such trials, has hitherto " kept a fairly tight rein on media contacts " he says, because of worries about a possible premature leak and " exposure to sensationalist media inquiries. "
See
UK Addiction Specialist Says, " Cannabis shouldn’t be denied to deserving cases
just because of the USA’s ineffective worldwide " war on drugs " during the last 80 years. "

In particular, Dr Notcutt has been meticulous about dissociating himself and the trials from hard-core cannabis legalisation campaigners.

He is careful to demarcate 'medical' from 'recreational' perspectives.

" We had to steer a difficult path at times. The issue is now accepted as totally separate, as with heroin. There is actually no need for a change in the law for medical uses,' " he says.

Dr Notcutt's initial curiosity about cannabis as a potential pain reliever dates back to when he worked in Jamaica during the 1970's.

Caribbean research

'I have long been interested in this field of research, having been aware of the therapeutic use of cannabis in the Caribbean for glaucoma and for psychiatric patients being weaned off alcohol.'

'Until now, it's something I could never pursue due to past problems of cannabis illegality and its non-status as a medicine in the UK,' he says.

'Until now, we haven't been able to conduct proper clinical tests, since you can't use herbal 'cannabis smoked in a joint or taken orally for such purposes.'

'It has been a long haul from the wilderness but I am really excited that the decks have now been cleared and that our unit is one of the first to get going on trials which should then take off all over Britain.'
He welcomes the fact that the past couple of years have seen a more enlightened attitude to looking into the medical value of a drug which has been used for pain relief for around 5,000 years.

The plans are to begin with volunteer patients suffering from multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, severe pain and spasticity. MS in particular is of interest to Dr Notcutt. There are many MS sufferers who have avoided cannabis simply because of the legal problems, but who should perhaps gain access to it legally in the form of a proper medicine.
See
Israeli Pharmaceutical Company Issues Press Release On Use Of Cannabinoid For MS

Dr Notcutt believes it is wrong to believe that debilitating illness sufferers would enjoy the same sensations from any drugs as do recreational users - or indeed that they would succumb to addiction or irresponsibly high doses.

'The majority of people who smoke cannabis for pain relief would do so to the point where they achieve just that and no more. There's no point in anybody being incapacitated with pain opting to become incapacitated with cannabis,' he says.
See

He stresses that he ventured into this field in the 1990s purely from a pain perspective, aware that cannabis had been used for its analgesic properties prior to the arrival of injectable morphine in the mid 1850s and aspirin at the turn of the century.

As a pain relief consultant, he found himself still faced with many untreatable patients and started wondering again about cannabis, which he recalled was still prescribable when he qualified in 1970, prior to the fashion for prescribing benzodiazepines.
See
UK Victims of Tranquilizers Urge That " Far Safer " Medical Cannabis Be Made Available -- IoS
 " More people died from benzodiazepine usage than from such drugs as heroin and cocaine. "

Untreatable patients

Dr Notcutt's interest in suggesting that cannabis should be examined more closely for its analgesic properties using modern techniques was a stand which he admits led him to being 'wheeled out as an unofficial spokesperson every time cannabis came up as a subject.

I alone was putting my head above the parapet,' he adds. Not until 1997 did a BMA report suggest looking into the therapeutic uses of cannabis.' The issue then started to gain momentum, followed in 1998 by a positive House of Lords scientific sub-committee investigation and in 1999 by the US's Institute of Medicine urging more clinical research into the matter.

'As I became more public, more patients, especially those with MS, opened up to me and I discovered a huge underclass out there quietly smoking cannabis for pain relief - and preferring it over morphine.

'It made me wonder, what's going on? People want the drug I don't prescribe! It made me want to find out more about cannabis.'

He saw little headway being made by either the Government or a synthetics-focused pharmaceuticals industry and wanted to initiate his own research with the aid of a pharmacist and pro-cannabis patients.

This drew interest from Dr. Geoffrey Guy, founder of GW Pharmaceuticals, who suggested approaching the Home Office and Medicines Control Agency to work through the associated bureaucracy.

Relevant authorities

Recalls Dr Notcutt: 'He seemed to know how to deal with the relevant authorities and within a year had set up a company and secured licences to produce plant material, extract the active ingredient and formulate it as a proper medicine. This was the major step forward we needed.'

The next stage was to investigate delivery systems. The original idea was to mimic inhalation but technical problems led to a sublingual approach, which has been tested in Phase I trials.

Eventually, he sees no reason why delivery should not be diversified. No time-scale has been placed on the trials, with no schedule for published results. The preference is to approach the matter with existing patients with the aim of building up evidence that cannabis has a place in pain therapy.

Dr Notcutt cautions that the primary goal is very basic research establishing the dosage range, safety profiles and efficacy of the drug, especially when used sublingually.

'We'll be asking patients questions such as " Does it work for your symptoms? Does it work as well as when you smoke it? What side-effects do you experience? How is your mood affected? Can you walk further and be more active at home? "

'These are quality of life issues for people with chronic unremitting pain - those people that modem medicine currently fails very badly.

'Pain relief hasn't seen substantially new drug in the past 25 years, so it is exciting to think that suddenly we may be presented with a new means of relieving and managing intractable pain.'

Individual patients

Due to problems of patient homogeneity, with varying symptoms and etiology, Dr Notcutt had to design a trial where he could look at patients individually as their own double-blinded placebo controls.

'These are single patient studies, which should build up a pattern of results that can gradually provide us with useful indicators as to the therapeutic efficacy of cannabis,' he says.
(MarijuanaNews note: -- Revised July 21, 2000 -- The IOM report paid lip-service to single patient studies, but essentially ignored the eight legal DEAland medical marijuana patients, each of whom are supplied 300 joints per month by the Federal government. [The testimony of one of the eight of the eight was included in the report.] They are technically in an " Investigative New Drug " program, but there has never been any attempt to study their sometimes amazing results.

Of course, the Drug Czar explicitly rejected single patient studies, saying that nothing could be learned from them. That is untrue. Rather, the government would not like what it would learn from the legal eight, so it ignores them. Good for them. Bad for everyone else.

However, there is often a real value to " N of 1 " -- single patient studies, especially with rare disorders. And of course, such studies are of great value to the patients. Not that they matter to the government.)

An important argument, he adds, is that there has been no recorded proven death from cannabis. 'Compared with other drugs in use, cannabis offers almost totally predictable side-effects - and they are less serious ones than with, say, morphine.

'Or take the widely prescribed NSAIDS anti-inflammatory drugs – they have been causing 2,000 fatalities a year. That, it could be argued, really puts things into perspective.'
